abstract: The diversification of peptide signaling systems has been a major driver of metazoan evolution and biological complexity. The insulin superfamily, which includes insulins, insulin-like peptides, relaxins, and insulin-like growth factors, is an ancient group of peptide hormones that regulate development, growth, metabolism, and reproduction across Metazoa. Yet our understanding of the evolutionary origin of insulin signaling and the full extent of insulin superfamily diversity remain incomplete, particularly in invertebrates. Here, we performed a large-scale sequence and structural investigation of the insulin superfamily by mining public databases with sequence- and structure-based computational analyses to build a final dataset of 7,020 insulin-family sequences. Insulin-like peptides were present in all metazoan lineages except Porifera and Ctenophora. The absence of an identifiable canonical insulin ligand in Porifera is particularly intriguing because insulin receptors are present, raising questions about the receptors ancestral function and the evolutionary origin of its ligand. We further identified 12 distinct structural classes of insulin-superfamily peptides, with the greatest diversity in invertebrates, marking these lineages as a major source of insulin scaffold innovation. Together, these findings provide new insights into the origin and diversification of insulin signaling, establish a framework for understanding insulin superfamily evolution, and offer a resource for the discovery and engineering of therapeutic insulin analogs inspired by natural diversity.
